In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the neural correlates of learning from speech are characterized by an increase in the local synchronization of neuronal assemblies in the gamma band, which is accompanied by an increase in long-range synchronization in the theta band.

the neural mechanisms underlying language acquisition may be characterized by the synergic engagement of two types of synchronization mechanisms: one local and item-based, which may be sustained by gamma activity; and another long-range, rule-based, which may depend on theta activity.

the neural dynamics underlying rule extraction from speech input are characterized by a complex interplay of different oscillatory frequencies and brain regions, which may reflect the different cognitive functions that are involved during language acquisition.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the initial exposure to a novel language activates a complex network of brain regions that are involved in different aspects of the learning process.
the gamma band synchrony, which is related to selective attention, is a necessary condition for word learning.
the learning of the embedded rules of the artificial language was supported by the long-range synchronization of neuronal ensembles, which was not present during the initial exposure.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the neural mechanisms sustaining rule extraction from speech are not limited to a local process, but require a long-range synchronization mechanism.
